newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Brinson sees investment industry going more global.
newsitem.headline: Brinson sees investment industry going more global.

text.p: U.S.-based international asset manager Gary Brinson said he expects the investment industry to increasingly favour global management strategies in the future.
He also warned against inflated expectations for market performance which may harm the industry in future.

"As we move into the 21st century, money management firms will increasingly be oriented toward working off (a) global market portfolio," he said, speaking at a panel here sponsored by the Financial Management Association International.

Brinson heads SBC Brinson, the Chicago-based global asset management unit of Swiss Bank Corp. He also is a member of SBC's group executive committee. Brinson Partners was acquired by Swiss Bank Corp in 1994.

Following a reorganisation at SBC last year, the Brinson division now oversees SBC's global institutional asset management operations. It manages $120 billion in assets worldwide, with a staff of 600 in 10 locations.
A comparison of a single "segment" -- he used the U.S. equity market as an example -- produced significantly lower returns over a 15-year period than a global portfolio with comparable volatility.
Brinson said organisation in the industry will also require a global platform. Money managers, reflecting the trend, will come increasingly from multicultural, multilingual backgrounds.
He said that evaluation of a company was more difficult as companies become more global: "In effect, the demise of these country factors... makes accounting data even more suspect."
"Our approach is cash-flow driven," he said, adding that "I think on a worldwide basis, it is the only hope you have of getting any comparability."

He said a challenge to active investors was to understand which companies were "conscious of economic value-added" versus those which "are just interested in doing whatever the accountants will allow them to do in terms of putting numbers through the income statement."
With respect to what panel speakers saw as a growing star cult among money managers -- some compared top managers to "football stars" -- Brinson joined in expressing caution.
"We are starting to see all of the wrong signs here," Brinson said.
He said money management could become more difficult in the future but this was not to say there would be negative returns.
"I am simply suggesting that maybe we will get into an environment where these grandiose real returns fall back to more normal levels," he said.
